forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Tendring repaid a maturity loan to the PWLB in September 2026 using its own cash, not new borrowing
news_drafts.lead:
Tendring District Council repaid a maturity loan from the Public Works Loan Board (PWLB), the government's lending arm for councils and the source of most council borrowing, in September 2026. The council's Quarter 2 2026/27 finance performance report, which went to Cabinet on 13 November, says the repayment was "funded via internal borrowing". That means it used the council's own cash instead of taking out a new loan. The paper does not give the amount repaid.

The report states that no new external borrowing has been undertaken in 2026/27.

According to the paper, internal borrowing is being used until interest rates reduce, consistent with the council's treasury advisers' guidance.

news_drafts.headline: Tendring's main budget was £3.669m underspent against profile at end of July 2026, papers show
news_drafts.lead:
Tendring Council's General Fund Revenue Account was underspent by £3.669m against its profiled budget at the end of July 2026, according to a budget monitoring report (the in-year check of spending against budget) for the Cabinet meeting of 23 October. The General Fund is the account that council tax and business rates pay into, covering services other than council housing and schools.

A profiled budget is the annual budget spread across the months of the year, so the figure compares actual spending with what the council had planned to have spent by the end of July. The report describes the £3.669m as a net underspend, meaning the total after overspends and underspends on individual budgets are set against each other.

The report says the position reflects the timing of spending across budgets and the timing of Government reimbursements for housing benefit. It does not present the figure as a saving, and the papers give no full-year forecast alongside it.

findings.headline: Local government reorganisation timetable for all 20 areas sets shadow elections in May 2028 and vesting day on 1 April 2029
findings.detail: The report says the Government has concluded that the LGR policy and decision criteria are robust, with final decisions for county areas expected late 2026 or early 2027. It states the same implementation timetable applies to all 20 areas, with shadow elections in May 2028 and vesting day on 1 April 2029.
findings.matters: The vesting date is the point at which the district's finances, debt and reserves would transfer, so finance directors and lenders at councils in the same reorganisation process would want the fixed timetable.
findings.figures: 20 areas; shadow elections May 2028; vesting day 1 April 2029
findings.quote: The implementation timetable will be the same for all 20 areas: shadow elections in May 2028 and vesting day on 1 April 2029.

findings.headline: General Fund capital financing requirement is estimated to fall from £4.528m in 2025/26 to £4.217m in 2027/28
findings.detail: The report gives the council's estimated General Fund capital financing requirement, which falls each year across the three years shown. It states that the estimated General Fund MRP charge for 2026/27 is £0.250m, and that the MRP policy is unchanged for 2027/28 with no voluntary overpayment planned and no use of capital receipts to replace MRP.
findings.matters: The falling underlying borrowing need and the stated MRP charge show a finance director how the council's General Fund debt is being provided for, and a lender can see that no voluntary overpayment or receipts-funded reduction is planned.
findings.quote: The estimated General Fund MRP charge in 2026/27 based on the most up to date Capital Financing Requirement is £0.250m.

findings.headline: Council expects the Government's April 2027 collection reforms to increase arrears outstanding and defer income
findings.detail: The report sets out that extending the instalment window to at least 63 days after the first missed payment, capping liability order costs and adding a 21-day period after final notice may slow the move of accounts into recovery. It also notes that the move to 12-month billing will flatten the collection profile, with some income received later in the year. The council says the scale of the effect is hard to determine at this stage.
findings.matters: A finance director planning cash flow for 2027/28 needs to know that the council expects collection timing to shift, and a lender looking at a council's short-term liquidity would want to see that the council is flagging the change now.
findings.figures: at least 63 days after the first missed payment before instalment rights are lost; additional 21 days after final notice; reforms effective April 2027
findings.quote: This is likely to increase the value of arrears outstanding at any one time and defer income that councils would otherwise have collected earlier in the financial year.

findings.headline: Tendring proposes allowing working age LCTS claims to be backdated by up to 3 months from 2027/28, subject to consultation
findings.detail: The report says the change would align working age claimants with the three-month backdating already available to pension age claimants, where eligibility can be shown from an earlier date. The council states the cost cannot be readily quantified and will be part of the scheme's overall cost, and it will consult the major preceptors before a draft scheme goes to Cabinet on 11 December 2026.
findings.matters: Backdating is a change that adds to scheme cost in a way that is hard to predict, and other billing authorities considering the same change would want to know how Tendring is framing the uncertainty.
findings.figures: maximum backdating of 3 months; maximum working age discount 80%; 5,739 working age households receiving support at end September 2026
findings.quote: it is proposed to allow the backdating of claims for financial support made under the LCTS scheme by working age claimants.

findings.headline: Estimated 2026/27 cost of the LCTS scheme is £13.056m, broadly in line with the budgeted base position
findings.detail: The report puts the estimated annual cost of the Local Council Tax Support scheme at £13.056m as at early October 2026, with about 10% (£1.306m) falling to Tendring and the rest to the major preceptors. It states that each 5% change in the discount would gain or lose the council roughly £50,000 to £100,000 a year, and that the council does not propose reducing the discount to balance the forecast.
findings.matters: Finance directors weighing a means-tested support scheme against cost pressure can compare the sensitivity figure, and lenders can see that the council has ruled out using the discount rate as a balancing lever.
findings.figures: £13.056m total estimated annual cost 2026/27; approximately £1.306m (about 10%) to Tendring; £50,000 to £100,000 per year for every 5% change in discount; 80% maximum discount for working age claimants
